Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Objections
Claim 4 is objected to because of the following informalities: Grammatical error in line 1: “…wherein second leg…”. The suggested change is: “…wherein the second leg…”.  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim 14 is objected to because of the following informalities: Grammatical error in line 1: “…wherein second leg…”. The suggested change is: “…wherein a second leg…”.  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 14-16 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claim 14 recites the limitation …wherein second leg… in line 1. There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claim 17 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ahamad et al. (US20200199805).
Regarding claim 17, Ahamad et al. teaches a laundry machine (see abstract) comprising: a cabinet 12 defining an internal cavity 14 (see paragraph [0057], figure 2A); a lid 26 secured to a top of the cabinet 12 and configured to transition between open and closed positions, wherein the lid 26 covers an opening to the internal cavity 14 in the closed position and provides access to the opening in the open position (see figures 1-2B, paragraphs [0057]-[0058]); and a hinge 50, 60, 86 rotatably securing a lower corner of the lid 26 to the cabinet 12 such that the lid 26 transitions between the open and closed positions via the hinge 50, 60, 86, the hinge 50, 60, 86 comprising, a post 86 protruding upward from a top of the cabinet 12 and secured to the cabinet 12 (see figures 3-4, 29, 39-40, paragraphs [0066]-[0068]), and an L-shaped bracket 50, 60 disposed along a bottom of the lid 26, secured to the lid 26 and configured to rotatably engage the post 86 to transition the lid 26 between the open and closed positions (see figures 3-4, 29, 39-40, paragraphs [0060]-[0068]). Ahamad et al. teaches first and second opposing hinges rotatably securing first and second lower corners of the lid 26 to the cabinet 12, with each hinge comprising a post 86 (see figure 2A). Ahamad et al. does not explicitly teach that both opposing hinges comprise the L-shaped bracket. However, since Ahamad et al. teaches that the L-shaped bracket provides a rotational support and connection between the post and the lid it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the instant invention that both hinges may comprise the L-shaped bracket so as to provide the expected rotational support and connection between the post and the lid on both corners. Furthermore, it has been determined that the duplication of parts constitutes an obvious design choice to one of ordinary skill in the art absent persuasive evidence that a new and unexpected result is produced. In re Harza, 274 F.2d 669, 124 USPQ 378 (CCPA 1960).
Claims 1-5, 7-15 and 18-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ahamad et al. (US20200199805) in view of Jager et al. (US20210062560).
Regarding claims 1, 9-10, Ahamad et al. teaches a laundry machine (see abstract) comprising: a cabinet 12 defining an internal cavity 14 (see paragraph [0057], figure 2A); a lid 26 secured to a top of the cabinet 12 and configured to transition between open and closed positions, wherein the lid 26 covers an opening to the internal cavity 14 in the closed position and provides access to the opening in the open position (see figures 1-2B, paragraphs [0057]-[0058]); and a hinge 50, 60, 86 rotatably securing a lower corner of the lid 26 to the cabinet 12 such that the lid 26 transitions between the open and closed positions via the hinge 50, 60, 86, the hinge 50, 60, 86 comprising, a post 86 protruding upward from a top of the cabinet 12 and secured to the cabinet 12 (see figures 3-4, 29, 39-40, paragraphs [0066]-[0068]), and an L-shaped bracket 50, 60 disposed along a bottom corner of the lid 26 (reads on claim 9), secured to the lid 26 and configured such that the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 and lid 26 are rotatable about the post 86 to transition the lid 26 between the open and closed positions (see figures 3-4, 29, 39-40, paragraphs [0060]-[0068]). Ahamad et al. does not teach that the L-shaped bracket is configured to rotatably receive the post. Jager et al. teaches a laundry machine (see abstract) and that a post 110 secured to the cabinet 22 may comprise a pin 118 such that a bracket associated with the door 14 is configured to rotatably receive the post 110 in a notch 108, providing a rotational connection and improved versatility (see paragraphs [0002], [0025], [0030], [0042], [0045], figures 2-4). Since both Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. teach laundry machines with hinged doors it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the instant invention that the L-shaped bracket in Ahamad et al. may be configured to rotatably receive the post so as to allow for the expected rotational connection and improved versatility, as shown to be known and conventional by Jager et al.
Regarding claim 2, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 1. Ahamad et al. also teaches in figures 3-4, paragraphs [0059]-[0063] that the lid 26 includes an upper panel 32, a web 36 extending downward from a side edge of the upper panel 32, and a flange 34 extending inward from the web 36, and wherein the upper panel 32, web 36, and flange 34 collectively define a C-channel 48.
Regarding claims 3-4, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 2. Ahamad et al. also teaches in figures 3-4, paragraphs [0059]-[0063], that the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 includes first 54, 60 and second 52 legs, the first leg 54, 60 is disposed within a C-channel 48 defined along a peripheral edge of the lid 26, the second leg 52 is disposed along a back edge of the lid 26; and the second leg 52 rotatably engages the post 86. Hence, in the modified system, it is readily apparent that the second leg would rotatably receive the post (reads on claim 3) and that the second leg would define the notch in which the post is disposed (reads on claim 4).
Regarding claim 7, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 3. Ahamad et al. also teaches in figure 20, paragraphs [0073]-[0074] that the first leg 54, 60 includes alignment protrusions 276 extending therefrom, the flange 34 defines alignment orifices 212, and the alignment protrusions 276 are configured to engage the alignment orifices 121 to position the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 relative to the lid 26.
Regarding claim 8, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 3. Ahamad et al. also teaches in paragraphs [0060], [0070], [0075], [0083] and figures 3-4, 12, 21, 29, 39-40 that the first leg 54, 60 defines tapped orifices 56, the web 36 defines through holes 80, and fasteners 82 extend through the through holes 80 and engage the tapped orifices 56 to secure the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 to the lid 26.
Regarding claims 11 and 14, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 10. Ahamad et al. also teaches in paragraphs [0060], [0070], [0075], [0083] and figures 3-4, 29, 39-40 that the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 includes first 54, 60 and second 52 legs, the first leg 54, 60 is secured to the lid 26, and the second leg 52 rotatably engages the post 86 (reads on claim 11). Hence, in the modified system, it is readily apparent that the second leg would define the notch in which the post is disposed (reads on claim 14).
Regarding claims 12-13, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claim 11. Ahamad et al. also teaches in paragraphs [0060], [0070], [0075], [0083] and figures 3-4, 12, 21, 29, 39-40 that the first leg 54, 60 defines tapped orifices 56, the lid 26 defines through holes 80 (reads on alignment orifices of claim 12), and fasteners 82 (reads on alignment protrusions of claim 12, as they extend from the first leg 54, 60) extend through the through holes 80 and engage the tapped orifices 56 to secure the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 to the lid 26.
Regarding claims 5, 15 and 19, Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. together teach the limitations of claims 4, 14 and 18. Jager et al. teaches in paragraphs [0002], [0025], [0030], [0042], [0045], figures 2-4 that an internal surface of the bracket partially defines the notch 108 (see opening of orifice 108 in particular) and defines a bushing orifice (see cylindrical internal portion extending from the opening of orifice 108) extending away from the notch 108, the post 110 includes a base 134 and a pin 118 protruding outward from the base 134, and the pin 118 is disposed within the bushing orifice such that the bracket and lid 14 are rotatable about the post 110 via the engagement between the pin 118 and bushing orifice. Hence, in the modified system, it is readily apparent that an internal surface of the L-shaped bracket would define the notch and bushing in which the pin of the post is disposed.
Regarding claim 18, Ahamad et al. teaches the limitations of claim 17. Ahamad et al. also teaches in figures 3-4, paragraphs [0059]-[0063], that the L-shaped bracket 50, 60 includes first 54, 60 and second 52 legs, the first leg 54, 60 is disposed within a C-channel 48 defined along a peripheral edge of the lid 26, the second leg 52 is disposed along a back edge of the lid 26. Ahamad et al. does not teach that the second leg rotatably receives the post. Jager et al. teaches a laundry machine (see abstract) and that a post 110 secured to the cabinet 22 may comprise a pin 118 such that a bracket associated with the door 14 is configured to rotatably receive the post 110 in a notch 108, providing a rotational connection and improved versatility (see paragraphs [0002], [0025], [0030], [0042], [0045], figures 2-4). Since both Ahamad et al. and Jager et al. teach laundry machines with hinged doors it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the instant invention that the L-shaped bracket in Ahamad et al. may be configured to rotatably receive the post so as to allow for the expected rotational connection and improved versatility, as shown to be known and conventional by Jager et al.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 6 and 20 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Claim 16 would be allowable if rewritten to overcome the rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), 2nd paragraph, set forth in this Office action and to include all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
The following is a statement of reasons for the indication of allowable subject matter: The closest prior art of record is Ahamad et al. (US20200199805). Ahamad et al. fails to teach/disclose all of the limitations of claims 6, 16 and 20. Further no other prior art was located that fairly suggested the claimed invention in whole or in part along with the requisite motivation for combination to anticipate or render the claimed invention obvious.
Conclusion
